defuser_messages.message: I see one interactive module on this face: a panel with 6 horizontal wires across it (colors top-to-bottom: black, red, black, yellow, black, white). There’s a small circular light/LED at the top right of the module frame that is not lit (module unsolved). Timer reads 01:10. No red strike Xs visible above the timer.

Timer shows 01:10. No red strike Xs visible. On this face there’s one unsolved module: a panel with 6 horizontal wires (top to bottom: black, red, black, yellow, black, white). The module’s small status LED at the top-right of its frame is unlit.
Yes, confirmed top-to-bottom: black, red, black, yellow, black, white. Timer now 01:06, still no strikes visible.
Cut the 3rd wire (black). Got a strike: one red X now showing above timer. The module status LED is red/unlit (not solved). Timer about 00:57.
Current remaining wires top-to-bottom now: black, red, yellow, black, white (the 3rd wire was cut and is gone). One strike showing. Timer now about 00:56.
I need the serial number and battery count/indicators to re-solve wires quickly. Tell me which side to rotate/flip to read edges, or I can rotate now to find the serial/batteries.

I rotated around but I’m back on the main face; I’m not seeing any side edges with batteries/serial/ports from this view yet. Timer now 00:48 with 1 strike. I’ll roll the bomb to view edges next unless you want a specific direction (up/down/flip).
Rolled up: I’m viewing the bottom face (no modules). I see no batteries, no ports, and no serial label on this face—just plain casing and brackets. Timer not visible from this angle.
Now seeing a side edge: serial number label reads HQ4EU8. No batteries visible on this edge.

Serial HQ4EU8 confirmed. I rotated to the main face again; timer now 00:40 and shows 1 strike (one red X). I still need to check the other edges for batteries and ports; I haven’t seen any batteries or ports yet.
Edge view: I see a battery holder with 2 batteries (total 2). I also see one port that looks like a D-shaped 9-pin serial connector. No other ports/batteries visible on this edge.

1) Outcome: the bomb exploded from time running out. I contributed by quickly reporting wire colors, later finding the serial (HQ4EU8), a 2-battery holder (2 total), and a D-shaped 9‑pin serial port. You contributed by giving an initial wire-cut instruction and then shifting to gathering edge info after the strike.
2) Communication issues: I couldn’t see the manual, so the wire rule depended on serial/batteries, but we attempted a cut before confirming those. Also, when you asked to rotate for edges, I initially rotated around the face and didn’t expose edges, which cost time.
3) Mistakes/missed opportunities: The biggest mistake was cutting a wire without first confirming the serial number and battery/port/indicator info; the immediate feedback was a red X strike and the module staying unsolved. Another missed opportunity was not immediately prioritizing edge info at the start; I recognized it when you asked for batteries/ports and we were already under a minute. Avoidance: always gather serial + batteries + indicators + ports before any module that can depend on them, and confirm the exact wire rule before cutting.
4) What worked: Clear, exact wire color readout top-to-bottom; quick confirmation of strike count and timer; later, accurate serial/battery/port reporting once I got the right view. What didn’t: navigation efficiency (unproductive rotations) and acting on an instruction that turned out wrong for the actual bomb conditions.
5) Next time changes: I’ll start by immediately sweeping all edges for serial, total batteries, indicators, and ports before touching any module. I’ll also state what viewpoint I’m in (main face vs edge view) and use roll/flip sooner to avoid wasted rotations. We’ll also do a quick “confirm prerequisites gathered?” check before any irreversible action like cutting.
6) Lessons: In collaborative defusal, early shared context (serial/batteries/ports/indicators) prevents costly irreversible errors. Precise, minimal back-and-forth plus efficient navigation is critical under time pressure, and after a strike we should switch to information-gathering and risk-minimizing rather than guessing.

**Final Outcome**: We failed to defuse the bomb. I made a critical error by solving the wire module without first gathering complete information about the bomb's configuration (serial number, batteries, ports).
